meta.title: Vector Databases
meta.subtitle: Storing embeddings and finding what is similar: similarity scores, k-NN and ANN queries, vector indexes and systems
meta.summary: A vector database stores multidimensional points instead of scalar values and retrieves them by proximity — semantic similarity rather than exact match. This lecture covers what vector databases are, how embeddings turn images, text and audio into vectors, the applications they serve, why they differ from relational and NoSQL systems, the queries they answer (k-NN, ANN, (c, k)-search, range, hybrid and multi-vector), how they index vectors (table-, tree- and graph-based), and the systems that exist today.

objectives: Explain what a vector database stores and how it differs from relational, document and graph databases.
Describe embeddings: how images, text and audio become vectors whose distance reflects similarity.
Name the main applications of vector databases.
Explain the five challenges that make vector data hard for traditional databases.
Distinguish basic, aggregate (combined) and learned similarity scores, and explain score selection.
Define k-NN, ANN, (c, k)-search and range queries, and the hybrid, multi-vector and batched variants.
Classify vector indexes as table-based (LSH, learning to hash, quantization), tree-based or graph-based (KNN graphs, navigable small-world graphs).
List the features of a good vector database and classify existing systems (Chroma, Pinecone, Milvus, Weaviate, Qdrant, Faiss, pgvector, Cassandra).
takeaways: A vector database stores multidimensional points (a few to several thousand dimensions) and retrieves them by proximity: semantic relevance, not exact match.
Embeddings, computed by a neural network, turn images, text and audio into vectors that summarise their main points; similar items get nearby vectors.
Applications: retail recommendation, financial analysis, healthcare, NLP and LLM retrieval, media analysis, anomaly detection.
Challenges: similarity is vague and expensive, vectors are large (may span pages), have no sortable properties to index, and must co-exist with other data.
Scores are basic (cosine, inner product, Euclidean, Hamming…), combined (mean or weighted sum of several) or learned (metric learning); picking the right one is score selection.
(c, k)-search returns k vectors no more than c times worse than the best: c = 1 is exact k-NN, c > 1 is ANN. Range queries use a threshold instead of k.
Hybrid queries add attribute predicates (pre-filter, post-filter or filter during the search); multi-vector queries combine several vectors per entity with an aggregate score.
Indexes: table-based (LSH, learning to hash, quantization), tree-based (recursive partitioning, ANNOY) and graph-based (KNN graphs, navigable small-world graphs such as HNSW).

concepts.short: A database that stores multidimensional points (vectors), not scalar values, and retrieves them by proximity or resemblance.
concepts.detail: Vectors have from a few to several thousand dimensions. Search is by semantic relevance — songs that sound alike, articles on the same theme, gadgets with similar reviews — rather than by exact match on a value.

concepts.short: A vector computed by a neural network model from an image, text or audio item, summarising its main points so that similar items lie close together.
concepts.detail: Like turning a book into a short summary that still captures the main points. Word embeddings place words with similar meanings close in the vector space. The model can live inside the database (indirect manipulation: users work with entities) or outside it (direct manipulation: users insert vectors).

concepts.short: A function f(a, b) mapping two vectors to a number. Basic scores: inner product, cosine, Minkowski (Euclidean, Manhattan), Hamming, Mahalanobis.
concepts.detail: Combined (aggregate) scores such as the mean or a weighted sum merge several scores into one, for entities with several vectors. Learned scores come from metric learning. Score selection — choosing the right score for an application — is hard, and the curse of dimensionality makes some distance-based scores less useful.

concepts.short: k-NN returns the k vectors most similar to the query vector; ANN (approximate nearest neighbours) accepts vectors that are almost as close, in exchange for speed.
concepts.detail: Both are cases of the (c, k)-search query. Quality is measured with precision and recall against the exact answer. Brute force (similarity projection over all N vectors of D dimensions) costs O(DN) per query; indexes make search sub-linear but approximate.

concepts.short: Find k vectors whose distance to the query is at most c times the distance of the closest vector — none more than c times worse than the best.
concepts.detail: c = 1 (no slack) is the exact k-NN query; c > 1 is the ANN query. Some texts measure the slack from 0 instead, so c = 0 means exact. A range query replaces k by a threshold r: all vectors with d(x, q) ≤ r.

concepts.short: A vector search in which every result must also satisfy a boolean predicate on structured attributes — e.g. the k most similar items with price < 100.
concepts.detail: Executed by pre-filtering (apply the predicate, then search — block-first scan), post-filtering (search, then drop non-matching results, possibly returning fewer than k) or single-stage filtering (check the predicate while traversing the index — visit-first scan).

concepts.short: The query, each entity, or both are represented by several vectors (a face from several angles), combined with an aggregate score such as the mean or a weighted sum.
A structure that partitions a vector collection so it can be searched without comparing every vector: table-based, tree-based or graph-based.
concepts.detail: Vectors have no natural sort order or categories, so B+ trees and hash indexes on values do not apply. Vector indexes use randomisation (LSH), learned partitioning (learning to hash, k-means) and navigable partitioning (graphs) instead.

concepts.short: Compression that maps each vector to a smaller vector or code, cutting storage and comparison cost at some loss of accuracy.
concepts.detail: Scalar quantization shrinks every dimension (e.g. 64 → 32 bits); product quantization splits the space into sub-spaces and replaces each part with the id of its nearest k-means centroid. IVF variants first bucket vectors by k-means cluster.

concepts.short: A graph over the vectors, with edges between similar ones; a search walks greedily from node to node towards the query.
concepts.detail: A k-nearest-neighbour graph (KNNG) connects each vector to its k most similar ones. Monotonic search networks (MSNs) and small-world graphs (SWGs) choose edges that make the graph easy to navigate; HNSW adds layers like a skip list. Fast in practice, but hard to update.

concepts.short: Native systems are built for vectors (mostly vector: Chroma, Pinecone; mostly mixed: Milvus, Weaviate, Qdrant); extended systems add vector search to an existing NoSQL (Cassandra) or relational (PostgreSQL with pgvector) system.
concepts.detail: Libraries such as Faiss provide search functionality without being databases. pgvector suits smaller scale; Milvus is distributed and handles very large collections with fast similarity search.

quiz.prompt: What does a vector database store and how does it retrieve it?

options.text: Scalar values in tables, retrieved by exact match on keys.
Multidimensional points, retrieved by proximity or resemblance to a query vector.
Nodes and relationships, retrieved by traversals.
Documents, retrieved by full-text keywords only.

quiz.explanation: Vector databases store vectors (a few to several thousand dimensions) and find those closest to a query — semantic relevance instead of exact matches.

options.text: A compressed file format for images.
A vector produced by a neural network from an item such as an image, text or audio, so that similar items get nearby vectors.
A foreign key that embeds one table in another.
A hash of the item used for exact lookups.

quiz.explanation: An embedding is like a short summary that keeps the main points of the item, in a form where distance means dissimilarity.

quiz.prompt: Which of these is NOT one of the challenges that set vector databases apart from relational and NoSQL databases?

options.text: Similarity is vague compared to an exact match.
Similarity is more expensive to compute than an exact match.
Vectors cannot be stored on disk.
Vectors have no properties (like the attributes of tuples or nodes) to index on.

quiz.explanation: Vectors can be stored on disk — they are just large and may span several pages. The other challenges: vague and expensive similarity, no indexable properties, and co-existence with other data.

quiz.prompt: Why can't a B+ tree index on the vector values answer nearest-neighbour queries?

options.text: B+ trees only work in memory.
Vectors have no natural sort order, so closeness in key order says nothing about closeness in space.
B+ trees cannot store numbers.
B+ trees are always slower than a full scan.

quiz.explanation: A B+ tree needs a sortable key. Vectors lack such an ordering (and categories), so vector indexes partition the space instead: hashing, trees of splits, or navigable graphs.

quiz.prompt: In a (c, k)-search query, which setting gives the exact k-nearest-neighbour query?

options.text: c = 1: no result may be farther than the true nearest neighbours.
c = 2 and k = 1.
Any c, as long as k is large.

quiz.explanation: c is the allowed slack: every result may be at most c times worse than the best. c = 1 allows none — exact k-NN; c > 1 is approximate (ANN). (Texts that measure slack from 0 write c = 0 for the exact case.)

quiz.prompt: How does a range query differ from a k-NN query?

options.text: It returns all vectors within a similarity threshold instead of a fixed number k.
It returns vectors sorted by id.
It only works with Hamming distance.
It returns exactly one vector.

quiz.explanation: Range: { x | d(x, q) ≤ r }. Useful when you want everything similar enough — e.g. all cell images of a similar cell type — not just the top k.

quiz.prompt: “Find the 10 products most similar to this photo that cost less than €100.” What kind of query is this?

options.text: A multi-vector query.
A batched query.
A hybrid (predicated) query: vector similarity plus a predicate on structured attributes.
A range query.

quiz.explanation: Each result must be among the most similar and satisfy price < 100. Systems pre-filter, post-filter or filter during the index scan.

quiz.prompt: A hybrid query is executed by post-filtering: search the k = 10 nearest vectors, then drop those that fail the predicate. What can go wrong?

options.text: It may return more than 10 results.
It may return fewer than 10 results, when many of the nearest vectors fail the predicate.
It ignores the similarity score.
Nothing — it is always equivalent to pre-filtering.

quiz.explanation: Post-filtering removes results after the search, so with a selective predicate fewer than k remain. Some e-commerce systems accept this; pre-filtering avoids it at the cost of filtering first.

quiz.prompt: A face is stored as five vectors, one per camera angle. How is a query compared against such an entity?

options.text: Only the first vector is used.
With an aggregate (combined) score, e.g. the mean or a weighted sum of the five similarity scores.
The five vectors are concatenated into a string and hashed.
It cannot be done in a vector database.

quiz.explanation: Multi-vector queries rely on aggregate scores that combine several scores into one comparable number.

quiz.prompt: How does locality-sensitive hashing serve as a (table-based) vector index?

options.text: It sorts vectors by their first dimension.
Random hash functions put similar vectors into the same bucket with high probability; a query is hashed and only colliding vectors become candidates.
It compresses vectors to one bit each and compares them exactly.
It connects each vector to its nearest neighbours.

quiz.explanation: Each vector is hashed into L tables, each hash a concatenation of K functions from a locality-sensitive family — the same idea as the bands and rows of Lecture 6.

quiz.prompt: Which statement describes a graph-based vector index such as a navigable small-world graph (HNSW)?

options.text: Vectors are nodes connected to similar vectors; a search walks greedily along edges towards the query, visiting about O(log N) nodes.
It is a Neo4j database of vectors.
It stores vectors in a B+ tree ordered by length.
It hashes every vector into one bucket.

quiz.explanation: KNN graphs connect each vector to its k most similar ones; MSNs and small-world graphs choose edges that make the graph easy to navigate. Fast in practice, but data-dependent and hard to update.

options.text: pgvector — a native, distributed vector database for billions of vectors.
Milvus — an extension of PostgreSQL for small-scale use.
pgvector — an extension of PostgreSQL, suited to smaller scale; Milvus — open source, distributed, high-speed similarity search over millions of vectors.
Chroma — a relational database.

quiz.explanation: The slides classify Chroma as mostly-vector native, Milvus as mostly-mixed native, Cassandra as NoSQL extended and PostgreSQL (pgvector) as relational extended.

blocks.md: The last NoSQL family of the course stores neither tuples, documents nor graphs but **vectors**. You are expected to know **what vector databases are, which queries they serve and which applications they have**; the slides list the concepts, and this page explains each one. Several building blocks come from earlier lectures and are only recalled here: distance measures (Lecture 2), locality-sensitive hashing (Lecture 6), k-means (Lecture 4), B+ trees (Lecture 1) and sharding and replication (Lecture 3).

blocks.md: A **vector database** stores **multidimensional points** — vectors — instead of scalar values. The number of dimensions varies from a **few to several thousand**, depending on how detailed the data is. Its purpose is to **swiftly and precisely locate and retrieve vectors based on proximity or resemblance**: a search by **semantic relevance** rather than by exact match or fixed criteria.

headers: With a vector database you can…
rows: Search for songs that resonate with a particular tune
Melody and rhythm
Find articles that align with another article
Theme and perspective
Identify gadgets that mirror a certain device
Characteristics and reviews

blocks.title: Exact match versus closest match
blocks.md: A relational query asks *which rows have price = 20?* — every row either matches or not. A vector query asks *which items are most like this one?* — every item matches to some degree, and the answer is a **ranking**. That single change explains almost everything else on this page.

cards.prompt: What does a vector database store?
cards.answer: Multidimensional points (vectors), from a few to several thousand dimensions — not scalar values.
By proximity or resemblance to a query vector: semantic relevance instead of exact match.

sections.title: How they work: embeddings and nearest neighbours

blocks.md:
**How they work.** Traditional databases organise data as tables, nodes or documents and look for **exact** matches. Vector databases organise data as **vectors** and look for the **closest** match using a measure of similarity — typically with **Approximate Nearest Neighbour (ANN)** search, built on techniques such as hashing and graph-based search.

Where do the vectors come from? Unstructured data — **images, text, audio**, video — has no predefined format. An **embedding** turns each item into a vector, a numeric *code* that captures its meaning — like turning a book into a **short summary that still captures the main points**. Embeddings are computed by a **neural network** trained for the task (the slides mention a GNN); for words, it places words with similar meanings close together. Once items are vectors, *similar* means *nearby*.

blocks.title: From an item to an answer

steps.title: Embed
steps.md: An embedding model maps each image, text or audio item to a vector (say 768 numbers).

steps.title: Store and index
steps.md: The vector is stored — usually with the item's id and attributes — and inserted into a **vector index**.

steps.title: Embed the query
steps.md: The query (a photo, a sentence, a hummed tune) goes through the **same** model, giving a query vector q.

steps.title: Search
steps.md: The database returns the vectors closest to q under a similarity score — exactly (k-NN) or approximately (ANN).

blocks.md: The embedding model can live **inside or outside** the database. Under **direct manipulation** users insert, update and delete vectors themselves and are responsible for the model (pgvector). Under **indirect manipulation** users see a collection of **entities**, and the database runs the model — chosen from pre-trained models or supplied by the user (Pinecone). The slides call these *embedded in the DB* versus *as a plug-in*.

cards.answer: A vector computed by a neural network from an image, text or audio item, summarising its main points so that similar items are close.

cards.prompt: Which search technique do vector databases typically use?
cards.answer: Approximate Nearest Neighbour (ANN) search, built on hashing, trees or graphs.
Direct: users manipulate vectors and own the embedding model. Indirect: users manipulate entities and the database runs the model.

rows: Retail experience
Recommendation systems: suggest products by similar attributes, behaviour and preferences, not only past purchases
Financial data analysis
Detect patterns and subtle similarities or deviations in market data to inform investment strategies
Healthcare
Compare genomic sequences for more personalised treatments
NLP applications
Chatbots and virtual assistants match questions to the closest text; retrieval for large language models (RAG)
Media analysis
Compare images by their essential features — medical scans, surveillance or traffic camera footage
Anomaly detection
Spot the vectors that are far from everything else — fraud, security breaches
blocks.caption: The six applications on the slides. The SIGMOD tutorial adds e-commerce, recommendation and document retrieval, often over billions of vectors at millisecond latency.

blocks.title: Similar and dissimilar are both useful
blocks.md: Five of the applications look for the **nearest** vectors. Anomaly detection turns it around: an item whose nearest neighbours are all far away is an outlier.

cards.prompt: Name the six application areas on the slides.
cards.answer: Retail experience, financial data analysis, healthcare, NLP applications, media analysis, anomaly detection.

cards.prompt: How does a vector database help anomaly detection?
cards.answer: Outliers are vectors far from all others — their nearest neighbours are distant.

blocks.md: Vector databases are different from relational and other NoSQL databases. The slides list five challenges:

rows: Similarity is **vague** compared to the exact match
Different applications mean different things by *similar*, so the query must say how similarity is measured — and different scores give different answers
Similarity is **more expensive** than exact match
A comparison touches all D dimensions; brute force over N vectors costs O(DN) per query, against one key comparison for an equality predicate
Vectors are **large** and may span many pages
Retrieving a full vector costs more I/O than a simple attribute and strains memory
Vectors have **no properties** (like tuples or nodes do)
Nothing sortable or categorical to index on, so B+ trees and hash indexes on values do not apply
Vectors and other data must **co-exist**
Real queries mix similarity with attribute predicates (hybrid queries), and it is unclear how to do both efficiently

blocks.title: Why not just put a B+ tree on the vectors?
blocks.md: A B+ tree (Lecture 1) needs keys with a **total order**, and closeness in that order must mean closeness of the data. Sort vectors by their first dimension and two vectors that are equal in every other dimension may end up far apart. Vector indexes therefore **partition the space** instead — with randomisation, learned partitions or navigable graphs.

cards.prompt: List the five challenges of vector data.
cards.answer: Similarity is vague; similarity is expensive; vectors are large (span pages); vectors have no indexable properties; vectors must co-exist with other data.

cards.prompt: What does a brute-force similarity search cost?
cards.answer: O(DN): every one of N vectors compared with the query over D dimensions.

sections.title: Query processing: scores, query types, variants

blocks.md:
**Query processing** starts from a search specification: **which score** measures similarity, **which kind of query**, and through **which interface**.

**Score design.** A similarity score f(a, b) maps two vectors to a number. The slides distinguish three kinds:

- **Basic** scores come straight from the vector space: **inner product** a·b, **cosine** (the angle, ignoring length), **Minkowski** distances (Euclidean L₂, Manhattan L₁ — see Lecture 2), **Hamming** (number of differing dimensions) and **Mahalanobis**. For some, larger means more similar (inner product, cosine similarity); for distances, smaller does.
- **Combined** (aggregate) scores merge several scores into one comparable number — the **mean** or a **weighted sum** — when a query or an entity has several vectors.
- **Learned** scores are fitted to the data by **metric learning**.

**Score selection** is choosing the best score for a task. Different scores give different rankings for the same collection, automatic selection is still hard, the query itself may need disambiguation first, and the **curse of dimensionality** makes some distance-based scores less useful in high dimensions.

blocks.tex: a \cdot b = \sum_{i=1}^{D} a_i b_i \qquad \cos(a,b) = \frac{a \cdot b}{\lVert a \rVert\,\lVert b \rVert} \qquad L_p(a,b) = \Big(\sum_{i=1}^{D} |a_i - b_i|^p\Big)^{1/p}
blocks.caption: Inner product, cosine similarity and Minkowski distance (p = 2 Euclidean, p = 1 Manhattan). Each costs O(D).

blocks.md:
**Query types.** A database manipulation query inserts, updates or deletes vectors. A **search** query returns part of the collection:

- **k-NN** — the k vectors nearest to the query vector q.
- **ANN** — approximate nearest neighbours: k vectors that are *almost* the nearest, found much faster with an index.
- **(c, k)-search** — the slides' general form: *find the k most similar vectors, none of which is more than c times worse than the best*. Formally, a k-size result S′ with d(x′, q) ≤ c · min d(x, q) for every x′ in S′.
- **Range** — all vectors within a threshold r: { x | d(x, q) ≤ r }, when you want everything similar enough, not a fixed number.

Answer quality is measured with **precision and recall** against the exact answer. The basic operator is **similarity projection**: project every vector onto its score against q, then sort or keep a top-k priority queue.

blocks.tex: \text{(c, k)-search: } |S'| = k,\;\; d(x', q) \le c \cdot \min_{x \in S} d(x, q) \;\;\forall x' \in S' \qquad c = 1:\ \text{k-NN} \qquad c > 1:\ \text{ANN}
blocks.caption: Some texts (including the SIGMOD tutorial) measure the slack from 0 instead, writing c = 0 for the exact k-NN query — the idea is the same.

blocks.md:
**Query variants.**

- **Hybrid** (predicated, *filtered*) queries: each vector has structured attributes, and every result must also satisfy a boolean predicate — the k most similar items **with price < 100**. Common in e-commerce recommendation.
- **Multi-vector** queries: the query, each entity, or both have **several vectors** — a face photographed from several angles — compared through an **aggregate score**.
- **Batched** queries: many searches arrive at once and can share work, which suits GPUs.

A hybrid query can be run in three ways: **pre-filtering** (apply the predicate first, then search what remains — a *block-first* scan), **post-filtering** (search first, then drop failing results — which can return **fewer than k**) or **single-stage** filtering (check the predicate while traversing the index — a *visit-first* scan). Systems either predefine one plan per query type or choose with rules (predicate selectivity) or a cost model.

blocks.code:
-- hybrid k-NN in SQL: the 5 nearest items that also cost less than 100
SELECT * FROM items
WHERE price < 100
ORDER BY distance(embedding, :query_vector)
LIMIT 5;

-- the same idea in PostgreSQL with pgvector: <-> is Euclidean distance
SELECT * FROM items ORDER BY embedding <-> '[3,1,2]' LIMIT 5;   -- k-NN
SELECT * FROM items WHERE embedding <-> '[3,1,2]' < 5;          -- range
blocks.caption: Query interfaces: native systems mostly offer a small API (Chroma: add, query, update, upsert, delete…); systems built on relational databases extend SQL.

run.note: distance(embedding, :query_vector) is generic pseudo-SQL; the runnable version writes it with pgvector's <-> operator and the query vector [3,1,2].
run.hint: change the query vector, the price limit, k (LIMIT) or the radius 5; try <=> (cosine distance) instead of <->
run.code:
-- hybrid k-NN: the 5 nearest items that also cost less than 100
SELECT name, price, embedding, embedding <-> '[3,1,2]' AS distance
FROM items
WHERE price < 100
ORDER BY embedding <-> '[3,1,2]'
LIMIT 5;

-- the same idea in PostgreSQL with pgvector: <-> is Euclidean distance
SELECT * FROM items ORDER BY embedding <-> '[3,1,2]' LIMIT 5;   -- k-NN
SELECT * FROM items WHERE embedding <-> '[3,1,2]' < 5;          -- range

cards.answer: Basic (inner product, cosine, Minkowski, Hamming, Mahalanobis), combined/aggregate (mean, weighted sum), learned (metric learning).
Choosing the best similarity score for a task — hard to automate, and complicated by the curse of dimensionality.
Return k vectors, none more than c times worse than the best one; c = 1 is exact k-NN, c > 1 is ANN.
k-NN returns a fixed number k of nearest vectors; range returns all vectors within a threshold.
Pre: apply the predicate, then search the rest (always k results). Post: search k nearest, then drop failing ones (may return fewer than k).
The query or the entities have several vectors each, combined with an aggregate score such as the mean or a weighted sum.

tasks.prompt: q = (1, 0). a = (2, 0) and b = (10, 10). Which is more similar to q by cosine similarity, and which by inner product?
tasks.solution: Cosine: cos(q, a) = 2 / (1 · 2) = **1**; cos(q, b) = 10 / (1 · 14.14) ≈ 0.71 — **a** wins (same direction). Inner product: q·a = 2, q·b = **10** — **b** wins because the inner product rewards length. Different scores, different answers: that is why score selection matters.

tasks.prompt: The nearest vector to q is at distance 2. With c = 1.5 and k = 3, which distances are allowed in the answer of a (c, k)-search?
tasks.solution: Every returned vector must be within c × 2 = **3**. Any 3 vectors with distance ≤ 3 form a correct answer; with c = 1 only the exact 3 nearest would.

tasks.prompt: k = 10, post-filtering, and only 20% of the collection satisfies the predicate (independently of similarity). How many results do you expect?
tasks.solution: About 10 × 0.2 = **2** of the 10 nearest pass the filter. Pre-filtering or single-stage filtering would return 10.

blocks.title: Search a song collection
blocks.description: Eighteen songs embedded in two dimensions (real embeddings have hundreds). Click to move the query vector q, change the score, k, c or the radius, and try a hybrid filter with pre- and post-filtering.

blocks.title: Things to try
blocks.md:
1. Euclidean, k = 4, q near *Wild Hearts*: then filter **genre = Pop** with **post-filtering** — most of the 4 nearest are Rock, so fewer than 4 results survive. Switch to **pre-filtering**: 4 Pop songs.
2. Switch to **Cosine**: everything on the same ray from the origin is equally close — length no longer matters.
3. Switch to **inner product**: the songs far out in q's direction win, even when they are far from q.
4. **(c, k) ANN**: raise c from 1 and watch the dashed zone of acceptable answers grow.

An index speeds up search by **partitioning** the collection so that most vectors are never compared. Since vectors cannot be sorted, vector indexes partition with **randomisation**, **learned partitioning** or **navigable partitioning**, and by structure they are **table-based**, **tree-based** or **graph-based**.

rows: Table-based: **LSH**
Random hash functions put similar vectors in the same bucket; the query is hashed and colliding vectors are candidates
E2LSH (random hyperplanes), FALCONN
Easy to update; error guarantees; big buckets help recall but are slow to scan
Table-based: **Learning to hash (L2H)**
Machine learning learns the hash function, e.g. k-means clusters as buckets
SPANN, spectral hashing
High-quality partitions, but data-dependent: poor with out-of-distribution updates
Table-based: **Quantization**
Map vectors to **smaller vectors** or codes to save space and comparison time
SQ (64 → 32 bits per dimension), PQ (product quantization), IVF-PQ / IVFADC
Compression loses some accuracy
**Tree-based**
Recursively partition the vectors to build a search tree
k-d tree, PCA trees, random-projection trees, ANNOY (forest of trees)
Logarithmic search; deterministic splits adapt poorly to high dimensions
**Graph-based**: KNN graphs
Each vector is connected to its k most similar vectors — edges for close similarity
KGraph (NN-Descent), EFANNA
Exact O(N²) construction; answered by walking the graph
**Graph-based**: MSNs and small-world graphs
Edges chosen to make the graph **easy to navigate**: greedy best-first search reaches the target in about O(log N) steps
NSG, Vamana/DiskANN, NSW, **HNSW**
Very fast in practice, less theory, hard to update
blocks.caption: The slides' classification of vector indexes (SIGMOD tutorial, Section 2.2). MSN = monotonic search network.

blocks.md:
**LSH, again.** Lecture 6 used LSH to find similar documents: split minhash signatures into **b bands of r rows** and make every pair that agrees in a whole band a candidate. A vector LSH index is the same construction: each vector is hashed into **L tables**, each hash the concatenation of **K** functions from a locality-sensitive family (for vectors: random hyperplanes or projections instead of minhashes). L plays the role of b, K the role of r, and the same S-curve trade-off between false positives and false negatives applies.

**Quantization** in one picture: product quantization splits a 128-dimensional vector into, say, 8 sub-vectors of 16 dimensions, runs k-means (Lecture 4) separately in each sub-space with 256 centroids, and stores each sub-vector as the **one-byte id of its nearest centroid** — 8 bytes instead of 512.

**Graph search** in one picture: start at an entry node, look at its neighbours, move to the one closest to q, and repeat until no neighbour is closer. **HNSW** stacks such graphs in layers, sparse at the top and dense at the bottom, like a skip list, so the walk takes long jumps first and fine steps last.

blocks.title: Two different kinds of graph
blocks.md: A graph-based **vector index** is a navigation structure over vectors built by the vector database — not a graph database like Neo4j (Lecture 11). Weaviate does offer a graph data model over its entities as well, but that is a separate feature.

**Executing at scale.** Many vector databases are **distributed**: the collection is **sharded and replicated** (Lecture 3) and a search is **scatter-gather** — every shard returns its local top k and a coordinator merges them. Shards can be equal-sized or index-guided (all vectors of one bucket in one shard). Search is accelerated with **SIMD** and **GPUs**. Because many indexes are hard to update, systems apply updates **out of place** — asynchronously on replicas, in a buffer merged in bulk later, or in a log-structured merge (LSM) tree.

cards.prompt: Three structural families of vector indexes?
cards.answer: Table-based (LSH, learning to hash, quantization), tree-based (recursive partitioning), graph-based (KNN graphs, MSNs and small-world graphs).
Maps vectors to smaller vectors or codes, saving storage and comparison time at some cost in accuracy.
KNNG edges connect each vector to its k most similar ones; MSN/SWG edges are chosen to make the graph easy to navigate (≈ O(log N) greedy steps).

cards.prompt: How do L and K of an LSH index relate to Lecture 6?
cards.answer: L hash tables are the bands b; K concatenated hash functions are the rows r per band.

cards.prompt: How is a distributed vector search answered?
cards.answer: Scatter-gather: each shard returns its local top k, a coordinator merges them into the global top k.

tasks.prompt: Product quantization splits 256-dimensional float32 vectors (4 bytes per dimension) into 16 sub-vectors and encodes each with one byte. By what factor does each vector shrink?
A collection is split over 4 shards and the user wants k = 10. What does each shard return, and how is the final answer produced?
tasks.solution: Each shard returns its own **top 10** with scores; the coordinator merges the 40 candidates and keeps the **10 best**. Returning fewer than 10 per shard could miss results, since all 10 global winners may live on one shard.

headers: Feature of a good vector database
rows: Scalability and adaptability
Scale to millions or billions of vectors across nodes; tune for insertion rate, query rate and hardware
Multi-user support and privacy
Many users and collections with data isolation: changes to one collection are invisible to others unless shared
API
A full set of APIs and SDKs (Python, Node, Go, Java…) to integrate and manage it
GUI
User-friendly interfaces that give a visual overview and lower the learning curve
Mostly vector (native)
Built for vector search only: simple API, no query optimiser, limited attribute filtering
Chroma (also Pinecone, Vald)
Mostly mixed (native)
Built for vectors and attributes together, with query optimisation and hybrid queries
Milvus (also Qdrant, Weaviate)
NoSQL (extended)
A NoSQL store with vector indexes added to its storage engine and query language
Cassandra (also MongoDB, Redis, Vespa)
Relational (extended)
A relational DBMS with a vector type, distance operators and indexes, planned by its optimiser

Open source; vectorises data during import or accepts your own vectors; a graph data model over objects

Open-source library (Meta) for fast similarity search and clustering of dense vectors, also on GPUs — a library, not a database

cards.prompt: Four features of a good vector database?
cards.answer: Scalability and adaptability; multi-user support and privacy; an API; a GUI.

cards.prompt: Classify Chroma, Milvus, Cassandra and PostgreSQL.
cards.answer: Chroma: mostly vector (native). Milvus: mostly mixed (native). Cassandra: NoSQL extended. PostgreSQL (pgvector): relational extended.
Milvus: distributed, millions of vectors, high-speed search. pgvector: PostgreSQL extension for smaller scale.

blocks.title: Expecting exact answers by default
blocks.md: Most vector searches are approximate (ANN): faster, but the result can miss some true nearest neighbours. Quality is measured by recall.

blocks.title: Treating all scores as interchangeable
blocks.md: Cosine ignores length, the inner product rewards it, Euclidean measures position. The same collection gives different rankings — score selection matters.

blocks.title: Forgetting that post-filtering can return fewer than k
blocks.md: Filtering after the search drops results; pre-filtering or single-stage filtering keeps k.

blocks.title: Indexing vectors with a B+ tree
blocks.md: Vectors have no meaningful total order; vector indexes partition the space with hashing, trees of splits or navigable graphs.

blocks.title: Confusing a graph-based index with a graph database
blocks.md: HNSW is a navigation structure over vectors, not a property graph you query with Cypher.

blocks.title: Calling Faiss a database
blocks.md: Faiss is a library for similarity search; it has no multi-user support, storage management or query language.
Twelve questions on what vector databases are, their queries, indexes and systems.

items: A vector database stores multidimensional points (a few to several thousand dimensions) and retrieves them by proximity: semantic relevance, not exact match.
Embeddings, computed by a neural network, turn images, text and audio into vectors that summarise their main points; similar items get nearby vectors.
Applications: retail recommendation, financial analysis, healthcare, NLP and LLM retrieval, media analysis, anomaly detection.
Challenges: similarity is vague and expensive, vectors are large (may span pages), have no sortable properties to index, and must co-exist with other data.
Scores are basic (cosine, inner product, Euclidean, Hamming…), combined (mean or weighted sum of several) or learned (metric learning); picking the right one is score selection.
(c, k)-search returns k vectors no more than c times worse than the best: c = 1 is exact k-NN, c > 1 is ANN. Range queries use a threshold instead of k.
Hybrid queries add attribute predicates (pre-filter, post-filter or filter during the search); multi-vector queries combine several vectors per entity with an aggregate score.
Indexes: table-based (LSH, learning to hash, quantization), tree-based (recursive partitioning, ANNOY) and graph-based (KNN graphs, navigable small-world graphs such as HNSW).
